# Handoff 02 - claude: framing panel B - the event-driven watch, and a browser engine inside C3

Date: 2026-10-14. Base commit: C3 `v0.2.1` (8a133f8). C3 is a Rust bridge that lets a coordinating agent (Claude
Code first; Codex CLI and other hosts through the same skills) consult reviewer models through their CLIs
(engines: codex, agy for Gemini, muse for Meta's Muse Code, http for OpenRouter/API models) with a roster, a
findings store, detached runs and panels. Read `README.md`, `plugin/skills/coordinate/SKILL.md` (the waiting rule)
and `docs/port/wave8-quota.md`.

## Question

Two designs before implementation. (A) The WATCH: a coordinator session waits for workers, detached panels, builds
and peer sessions by a wake every 20-30 minutes that keeps its prompt cache warm; most wakes find nothing and still
cost a full cached read of a large context. We want an event-driven watch inside the bridge that answers "did
anything change since <instant>?" so a wake can be skipped or answered in one line without reading the context.
(B) A BROWSER ENGINE: reviewers that exist only as web chats (through the user's own Chrome tab, user-land
adapters) as a C3 engine beside codex/agy/muse/http - the product rules are already decided by the operator (below);
the panel is asked about the architecture inside C3.

## Task state

- Done: detached runs and panels with `--status` / `--wait`; the waiting rule in the coordinate skill (a wake about
  every 20 minutes via the host's scheduler, small reads at each wake, an idle rule after two quiet wakes); the
  SessionStart hook line.
- Open (A): nothing in the bridge knows whether a wake is useful; the host's scheduler (Claude Code: a cron-like
  prompt, `ScheduleWakeup`, a `Monitor` on a file) can only fire or not fire.
- Open (B): no engine for web-only reviewers; the operator's rulings (from a panel of 2026-10-14 in the plugin
  repository, ROADMAP.md "Browser engine"): nothing site-specific in the product; adapters compiled to WASM from
  Rust as the primary form, JavaScript allowed behind ONE deny-by-default host API; draft-only by default (the
  adapter prepares, the user sends); pacing is rate limiting, never stealth jitter; a signed hash/pointer catalogue
  of adapters; a private plugin first; the public usefulness table ranks per adapter and vendor.
- Not in scope: the host's scheduler itself; any site-specific adapter; the measurement designs (panel A).

## Evidence

- `crates/c3/src/consult/detach.rs`, `crates/c3-cli/src/main.rs` (`--status`, `--wait`) - the status files a
  watch could fold.
- `plugin/skills/coordinate/SKILL.md` - the waiting rule as written for Claude Code (ScheduleWakeup ~1200 s).
- `crates/c3/src/engines/{codex.rs,subprocess.rs}` - the engine contract today: a CLI spawned with a prompt on
  stdin, a structured reply by output schema, a transcript, liveness and kill records (the recovery chain that the
  acceptance rounds hardened: "no kill without a record").
- `~/gemini-mcp` (the operator's prior art, outside this repository): a Chrome extension plus a WebSocket relay that
  drove a web chat from an MCP server.

## The coordinator's sketch (to be challenged)

(A) `c3 watch --task <t> --since <instant> [--worker-state <path>...]`: reads the status files of detached runs,
the tails of the named worker STATE files, the ledger's newest entry and the health journal, and prints ONE line:
`nothing since <instant> (next known event: <detached run budget end / quota reset>)` or `changed: <what>` - exit
code 0 nothing, 3 changed. The host's wake then runs this command first (a few hundred tokens) and reads the context
only on exit 3; a Monitor on the status directory can replace the periodic wake entirely where the host has one. A
`--next` hint lets the coordinator schedule the next wake at the earliest known event instead of a fixed period.

(B) An engine `browser` with the same contract as the others (brief in, structured reply out, transcript, kill
record): C3 starts a local relay (WebSocket, loopback only, a per-run token), the Chrome extension connects, an
ADAPTER (WASM, loaded from the signed catalogue by hash) runs inside the extension with a host API of a few calls
(open the chat URL, put text in the composer, read the reply stream, done) that is deny-by-default per capability;
default mode draft-only: C3 writes the brief into the composer and the user presses send; `--send` lets the adapter
send when the user allowed it once for that adapter; pacing by a token bucket per vendor; the reply is parsed by
the output schema like the others; the usefulness table keys on adapter + vendor.

## Alternatives weighed

1. **(A) the watch command + `--next` hint (the sketch)** - small; the host still has to fire the wake.
2. **(A) a long-lived `c3 serve` that pushes events** (a local socket the host's Monitor can read) - no wasted
   wakes at all; a daemon to keep alive and secure.
3. **(B) WASM adapters in the extension (the sketch)** vs **(B') the adapter runs in C3 and the extension is a dumb
   DOM bridge** (the host API is then C3's, the extension is tiny and auditable) vs **(B'') a Chrome DevTools
   Protocol driver without an extension** (no user-land install; fragile, against the "user's own tab" ruling).

Current preference: (A) 1 now, 2 later; (B) B' - the extension as a dumb, signed DOM bridge; the adapters as WASM
in C3's process with the deny-by-default host API there.

## Questions

- **Q1.** (A) What should the watch fold, and what is the cheapest reliable "next known event" the coordinator can
  schedule against? Where does a skipped wake lose something (a cache that expires, a worker that died silently)?
- **Q2.** (B) Where should the adapter run - the extension (WASM), C3's process (B'), or elsewhere - given the
  rulings (deny-by-default host API, draft-only, signed catalogue)? What is the minimal host API?
- **Q3.** (B) What must the engine record for the recovery chain (liveness, kill, a reply that never comes because
  the user did not press send)?
- **Q4.** A risk or a design we did not list, for either.

Answer by number. Keep it under 600 words.

---
name: coordinate
description: How the coordinator drives the c3 reviewer bridge from a Claude Code session - the invariants, the live-member rule, the bridge's own background means (--detach / --status / --wait / --kick), the coordinator record (CODEX_CONSULT_COORDINATOR), the worker-tier contract, and the supporting c3 commands (pack, explain, snapshot, index, router). Read it when running c3 as a coordinator session, not as a one-off consultation.
argument-hint: "[what you are coordinating]"
allowed-tools: Bash(c3:*), Read, Glob, Grep
disable-model-invocation: false
---

# Coordinate (c3)

The C3 port supports one coordinator host: **Claude Code**. This skill is the coordination
layer over the `c3` binary. (The multi-host coordination story â€” Codex CLI, Z Code, Kimi Code,
a plain shell â€” stays with the `codex-consult` PowerShell bridge and is deliberately not ported
here.) The consultation procedure itself is the `consult` skill; wiring reviewers is
`setup-providers`.

## Invariants

- **You are the coordinator and the judge by default.** Workers execute, reviewers advise, you
  decide and verify. Never redo a worker's work once it reports â€” read the report and verify in
  your own loop; what still needs checking is a new, scoped task.
- **One objective per worker.** Brief it precisely the first time: the objective, the exact
  files, the numbers its result is measured against, what it must not touch, the report shape. A
  launch, a wait and a re-brief cost more than a brief written once.
- **English to reviewers and workers.** Briefs, prompts and handoff titles are in English;
  source material in another language is translated or summarised, never pasted.
- **Wait without blocking; keep the prompt cache warm.** Poll a state file or `c3 consult --task
  <task> --status`; never sit in a blocking foreground wait longer than the shell tool's limit.
  After the cache's lifetime the next request re-writes the whole context, so a large context
  must not go cold by oversight.
  - *Running work* (keeps the wake armed, idle count zero): a worker or subagent that has not
    reported; a detached consultation or panel (start `c3 consult --task <task> --wait` in the
    background - its exit is the signal - or poll `--status`); a long shell job (a suite, a
    build); a window you gave another session, until it says it is done; an operator step with a
    named end ("I install it and come back"); a cooldown with a named end (a provider's
    `retry_after`, a quota window). Idle is only: none of these, and nothing can be done without
    the operator.
  - *The means in Claude Code:* a Monitor or a background wait is the primary signal; the
    `ScheduleWakeup` tool is the heartbeat - about 20 minutes (1200 s), armed at the first
    delegation or wait of the session and kept while running work goes on. Every wake: small
    reads only (a state file's tail, `c3 consult --task <task> --status`); one line when nothing
    finished. Anything finished or needing action is activity: act, and the idle count restarts.
  - *Idle:* idle wake 1 - one line in the state file ("idle since <time>"); idle wake 2 - write
    the handover on disk, stop the wakeups, and tell the operator in one line the cheap ways
    back: a fresh session from the state file; `/compact` is the operator's to run.
  - *Compaction* only at a wave boundary (the report is read, the state is on disk) and only
    while the cache is warm. In Claude Code the agent has no means to compact itself: while work
    runs, keep the context warm however long the wait; when idle, hand over as above.
- **Rate every consultation** once its reply is read (`c3 findings --task <task> --rate <n>
  --useful yes|partly|no`). A routed panel draws its seats from these marks.
- **Ask the operator before going on without a required reviewer** â€” when one the topic needs is
  out, or `--require` refuses the run, tell the operator who is out and until when.

## The live-member rule

While an `agy` or `muse` member runs (a single run or a panel member, detached or not), write
NOTHING under the collab directory or the working tree â€” `state.md`, notes and findings stores
included â€” and run no git command. Both engines are checked by evidence: a change during an
`agy` run FAILS that member; during a `muse` run it WARNS; either way the reviewer read a moving
target. This binds your workers too: hold a writing worker until `--status` says the run is
done, then write what you queued. (The `http` engine never touches the machine â€” it only warns.)

## The coordinator record

- The coordinator's session identity never reaches a reviewer child. `c3` scrubs the host
  markers (`CODEX_SESSION_ID`, the `CLAUDE_CODE_*` session ids, the messaging socket and token,
  `CLAUDE_PID`, `CLAUDE_EFFORT`, every `CODEX_SANDBOX*`, and the `ZCODE_*` / `ZCODE_PLUGIN*`)
  from every reviewer CLI and launcher probe. The ledger records the removed NAMES in
  `child_env_scrubbed`, never a value. The operator's own settings, the plugin roots and the
  provider keys are kept.
- The coordinator's identity is recorded once per run in the ledger `coordinator`
  `{provider, model, engine, host, source}`. `host` is `claude-code` when the Claude Code
  markers are present, else `unknown`. Set `CODEX_CONSULT_COORDINATOR` to `<provider> :: <model>`
  (optionally ` [<engine>]`), a roster position `#<n>` or a provider label to name the
  coordinator's own model; a reviewer the bridge seats that IS your model gets a warning (never a
  refusal), and an unparseable value is refused before anything starts. Keep the operator's value
  when it is set â€” do not guess your own.

## The bridge's own background means

Prefer these to the host's own backgrounding. Full mechanics and exit codes: the `consult`
skill's `reference.md`.

- `c3 consult --detach ...` â€” run a consultation or a panel in the background, return at once
  with the detach id, its status file and the come-back commands. Checked first: a refusal comes
  back immediately, nothing written.
- `c3 consult --task <task> --status [--id <id>]` â€” read status only, never blocks (0 done+usable,
  1 done with a failure or died, 2 running). `--status --prune` removes files of runs done/died
  > 7 days.
- `c3 consult --task <task> --wait [--id <id>] [--wait-timeout-sec <s>]` â€” block until done; keep
  `<s>` below your tool's command timeout.
- `c3 consult --task <task> --kick --member <NN> [--id <id>]` â€” stop ONE hung member; its partial
  is salvaged and the panel goes on. Ask the operator before kicking a merely-slow member.

Park a detached run in the task's `state.md` (the detach id, the brief path, the come-back
command); a later session finds it there and in the SessionStart line.

**Quota windows (wave 8).** Before a wave of reviews on a subscription plan, read the QUOTA column of
`c3 providers` (`5h 96% until 18:32; wk 15% until Oct 20`): a quota window at 98 % or more makes
the reviewer out until its reset, like a usage limit - ask the operator whether to wait or to go on
without that reviewer. Keep review threads small: prefer `--mode new` with a brief that names the
earlier reply over forking a large thread (a parent rollout over `CODEX_CONSULT_FORK_MAX_KB` is refused,
it would be replayed on every tool call); the bridge stops a run at `--budget` (90 % by default) with its
partial kept, and turns the reviewer's sub-agents off.

## Supporting c3 commands

- `c3 pack --brief <b> --out <o> [--focus <glob>] [--budget <n>] [--task <t>]` â€” build a
  sanitizing reviewer pack (with a `.pack.json` sidecar) for the `http` engine or for a chat
  model; the index feeds the periphery when present, else a lexical neighbourhood.
- `c3 explain --claim "<c>" [--focus <glob>] [--audience <who>] --yes` â€” an explainer pack for
  one claim. **It leaves the machine only after you confirm** (`--yes` skips the prompt).
- `c3 snapshot [--delta] [--depth 0-9] [--budget <n>] [--focus <glob>]` â€” a repository snapshot,
  optionally a git delta since the last full snapshot's anchor.
- `c3 index build|rebuild|query|stats` â€” the local code index (embedded SurrealDB, per project).
  Never required for a consultation; `query` is BM25 + reciprocal-rank with a bounded 1-hop
  expansion.
- `c3 router simulate|replay|priors|explain` â€” routing insight: `explain` prints the score table
  the next panel draw would use, one line per roster lineage; `replay` confirms a routed panel's
  seats from the ledger.
- `c3 telemetry status` (the on/off status and instance id), `c3 complain "<text>"` and
  `c3 forget-me` (the maintainer intake; both confirm before sending). Telemetry is on by
  default, carries outcome classes only â€” never task names, prompts, briefs, paths or keys â€” and
  `CODEX_CONSULT_TELEMETRY=off` switches it off.

## Worker-tier contract

Pick the tier by what the task needs; the names stay, the models behind them change.

- **Deep reasoning that needs judgment** (`opus-worker`) â€” novel code, multi-file debugging,
  build-and-fix loops. Writes.
- **Well-specified, pattern-following execution** (`sonnet-worker`, the default) â€” a known change
  across files, tests to a pattern, doc updates, running a suite and reporting. Writes.
- **Cheap read-only recon** (`haiku-worker`) â€” locating code, mapping a surface, log analysis,
  run-and-report. Never writes.

Delegate a chunk that is self-contained, heavy/noisy, or one of several independent pieces (fan
those out in one turn). A worker never starts or finishes the overall task and never commits
unless its brief says so.

# Wave 8 - quota windows (the plugin's wave 30, TECH_DEBT T15)

Spec: the plugin's `bade7cb..a162b8d` (`[Unreleased]` 0.6.2) - README "Quota windows and the reading

replay guard, the budget resolution, the budget watch rule, multi_agent, UUIDv7), `health::
quota_window_tests` (4: 99 % unavailable with its reset and the refusal, 84 % low quota, a past reset
and a 0.6.1 entry and newest-wins, the machine record class `""` round trip), `ledger` (the key order
and tri-states), `summary` (the `-Budget` and the new-thread hint), `telemetry::classes` (a budget stop
is class quota), `pending_liveness::the_budget_watch_stops_the_turn_at_the_quota_budget` (the real
spawn/kill path, a 200 ms poll).

## 8b - the equal-time tie (reviewer finding F46-1)

`endpoint_window` took a candidate only when its `observed_at` was STRICTLY newer, so at an equal
timestamp (the ledger writes `observed_at` without fractional seconds, ties are likely) the first
entry stayed: a 30 % observation could hide a 99 % one and the reviewer stayed available. The
recorded-observation selection and the live-rollout replacement now share ONE comparison
(`quota::window_obs_wins`): newer `observed_at` wins; at an equal instant the higher primary
`used_percent` wins, then the higher secondary (the rule `newer_wins` already applied to rollouts).
Tests: `endpoint_window_at_an_equal_time_keeps_the_fuller_window_in_both_orders` and
`the_live_window_replaces_a_lower_recorded_one_at_an_equal_time` (both failed before the fix).
`observed_at` comparison sites: `quota.rs` recorded selection (fixed), live replacement (fixed),
`newer_wins` (already correct); `health.rs` only consumes `endpoint_window` (n.a.); the machine-wide
record merge has no `observed_at` comparison (n.a.).

Plugin parity: `codex-consult-common.ps1` `Get-EndpointWindow` (lines ~6985 and ~6989) uses
`-gt $best.ObservedAt` for both the recorded and the live selection - the SAME tie. A plugin
TECH_DEBT candidate (not edited here).

## 8c - the equal-time merge per window (reviewer finding F48-1)

The 8b tuple rule (primary first) could hide a blocking weekly window: at an equal `observed_at`,
primary 40 % / secondary 99 % lost to primary 50 % / secondary 20 %. The coordinator's rule: at an
EQUAL `observed_at` the windows merge PER WINDOW - the endpoint's primary is the observation with
the higher primary `used_percent` (with that observation's reset), the secondary independently the
higher secondary (with its reset); a strictly newer `observed_at` still replaces both.
`quota::select_window` (recorded and live selection of `endpoint_window`, replacing
`window_obs_wins`) and `quota::merge_observation` (the sub-agent and account-rollout aggregation,
built on `newer_wins`, which still decides newer-or-not) apply it. Tests:
`endpoint_window_at_an_equal_time_merges_per_window_in_both_orders`,
`the_live_window_merges_per_window_with_a_crossing_recorded_one` (both assignments),
`merge_observation_keeps_each_fuller_window_at_an_equal_instant`; the 8b tests stay.
The plugin's T17 fix of the tie (see 8b) must use the same per-window rule.

## 8d - a total order for tied windows (reviewer finding F50-1)

At an equal `observed_at` and an equal `used_percent` the per-window pick kept the FIRST window's
reset, so a null or past reset could hide a future one by ordering. One comparator
(`quota::cmp_window_rank`, used by `select_window` for the recorded and live selections and by
`merge_observation`) now ranks two observations of the same window at the comparison time `now`:
(1) a known FUTURE reset beats a known PAST reset beats a missing (null) one; (2) the higher
`used_percent`; (3) the later `resets_at`; (4) identical - either. A strictly newer `observed_at`
still replaces both windows. Tests: `equal_shares_rank_by_the_reset_in_every_order`,
`the_live_window_ranks_a_future_reset_over_a_null_one_at_a_tie`,
`a_past_reset_never_hides_a_future_one_whatever_the_share`,
`the_tie_selection_is_the_same_for_every_permutation` (4 observations, all 24 orders).
The plugin's T17 fix must use this full ordering (future > past > null, then share, then later reset).

## 8e - one comparison instant, finite percentages (reviewer findings F52-1, F52-2)

The 8d rank depends on `now`, and each comparison sampled the clock on its own, so a reset crossing
from future to past DURING one aggregation (the rollout reads happen between merges) made the pick
order-dependent (A=(100 %, R), B=(99 %, S), C=(30 %, S), R < S). `now` is now sampled ONCE at the
top of each public entry point - `endpoint_window` (-> `endpoint_window_at`), `account_window`
(-> `account_window_at`), `codex_run_quota` - and passed as a parameter to `select_window`,
`merge_observation` and `cmp_window_rank` (no clock read inside the comparator); the health
evaluation hands the same `now_utc` to `endpoint_window_at` and to the "reset in the past" verdict.
F52-2: `finite_percent` treats a non-finite or out-of-range (outside 0..=100) share - a "NaN" /
"inf" text included - as an ABSENT window, in the window states (the block evaluation), the
selection and the rollout parser; the comparator uses `f64::total_cmp`. Tests:
`one_comparison_instant_makes_the_aggregation_order_independent` (A/B/C, all 6 orders, an instant
before R keeps A, one between R and S keeps B, both block),
`a_non_finite_percent_never_hides_a_valid_block`,
`the_tie_selection_is_the_same_for_every_order_of_six` (720 orders, a past reset and a NaN included).
The plugin's T17 fix needs the same single instant and the finite check.

## 8f - the account cache keeps raw observations, newer invalid windows do not replace (F55-1, F55-2)

F55-1: `account_window` cached only the WINNER picked at an earlier instant and returned it for 60 s,
so after that winner's reset a discarded equal-time observation that still blocked was lost. The
cache (per codex home) now holds the RAW observations of the account's rollouts
(`read_account_observations`); `account_window_at` runs the selection (`merge_observation`) at
every lookup with the requested `now`, the 60 s TTL only bounds how often the rollouts are read.
F55-2 (fail closed, per window): an observation with no VALID window is absent; a strictly newer
observation replaces a window only where its own window is valid, otherwise the older valid window
of that kind stays, and an older observation fills only the kinds the newer one lacks - in
`select_window` (recorded and live) and in `merge_observation`; at an equal instant the 8d rank
decides. Tests: `the_account_cache_selects_at_each_requested_instant`,
`a_newer_invalid_record_keeps_the_older_valid_window` (NaN / out of range, both orders, plus the
newer-partial case), and the permutation test now runs 5040 orders of seven observations (a
NaN-only newer record included). The tests that read `endpoint_window` are serialised with those
that switch the process-wide live source on (a flake of the shared global). The plugin's T17 fix
needs the same cache shape and the per-window validation.

## 8g - every window carries its OWN observation instant (reviewer finding F58-1)

Partial-window aggregation kept an older observation's window but stamped the aggregate with the
NEWER observation's instant, so a later comparison treated the retained window as newer than it
was: with t1 < t2 < t3, A = primary 30 % at t1, B = secondary 10 % at t3, C = primary 99 % at t2,
the fold A, B, C kept 30 % (B had promoted A's primary to t3) and A, C, B kept 99 %. Now
`Observation` carries `primary_at` / `secondary_at` (`window_at(kind)`: its own, else `at`),
`EndpointWindow` and `AccountWindow` carry `window_at: [primary, secondary]`, and a candidate window
is compared only with the instant of THAT retained window (strictly newer replaces, equal takes the
8d rank, older is kept; an invalid window has no instant and never replaces). The aggregate
`observed_at` / `at` is derived (the latest per-window instant) for display and the age of the
record, never for a replacement decision. The instants flow: rollout parse (`at` of the event) ->
`merge_observation` (per-window instants kept) -> `account_window_at` (`AccountWindow.window_at`
from the aggregate, over the raw cache) -> `endpoint_window_at` (recorded candidates carry their
entry instant on both windows, the live candidate its `window_at`) -> `select_window` (compares per
window with `EndpointWindow.window_at`). Tests: `partial_windows_keep_their_own_instants_in_the_recorded_selection`,
`partial_windows_keep_their_own_instants_in_merge_observation`,
`partial_windows_keep_their_own_instants_across_the_recorded_live_split`,
`distinct_instant_partial_windows_are_order_independent` (720 orders, distinct instants, partial
windows, a NaN-only one). The plugin's T17 fix needs per-window timestamps too.

## 8h - the per-window instants survive persistence (reviewer finding F60-1, supersedes F58-1)

8g kept each window's instant in memory, but `Observation::to_quota` wrote ONE aggregate
`observed_at`, so a recorded aggregate (the ledger's `quota`, the machine-wide health record - both
carry the quota object verbatim) lost the provenance: `endpoint_window_at` rebuilt both instants
from it, and an aggregate of A (primary 30 at t1) and B (secondary 10 at t3) labelled its primary
with t3 and beat C (primary 99 at t2). The quota record now carries two optional keys after
`observed_at`: `primary_observed_at` and `secondary_observed_at` (ISO, local offset), written by
`to_quota` only for a window that is present (a null quota keeps exactly `primary, secondary,
observed_at`). They are written wherever the quota is written (the ledger entry of a codex run, the
machine-wide record) and read by the recorded selection in `endpoint_window_at`; the aggregate
`observed_at` is only the LEGACY fallback of a record written before 8h (keys absent), and the
selected `EndpointWindow.quota` is re-stamped with them. Plugin compatibility: the oracle reads
only keys it knows; its one strict key check is on the NULL quota (`primary,secondary,observed_at`),
which is unchanged. Tests: `the_quota_record_carries_per_window_instants_through_ledger_and_health`,
`a_persisted_aggregate_cannot_promote_its_older_window` (both recorded orders and C live),
`a_legacy_record_without_window_instants_uses_the_aggregate_instant`. The plugin's T17 fix needs
the same two ledger fields.

## 8i - lossless instants, the imprecise rule, the legacy policy (reviewer finding F62-1)

8h stored each window's instant through a seconds-only formatter, so a recorded 99 % observed at
12:00:00.900 read back as 12:00:00 and an OLDER live 30 % at 12:00:00.100 looked strictly newer and
replaced it. Three rules now:
1. **Lossless**: `primary_observed_at` / `secondary_observed_at` are written as RFC3339 with the
   fractional seconds the instant has (`2026-10-13T12:00:00.900+00:00`; no fraction when it has none),
   in `to_quota` and in the re-stamp of `select_window`; read back exactly. The aggregate
   `observed_at` keeps its seconds-only format (compat).
2. **Imprecise compare** (`cmp_instants`): an instant without a fractional part is imprecise (a legacy
   aggregate, a second-precision record, a whole-second rollout stamp). If either side is, the two
   are compared at whole-second granularity: a recency win needs a strictly later whole second, the
   same second is a tie and the 8d rank decides (future reset > past > null, higher share, later
   reset). Both precise: exact. (A precise instant that happens to be exactly on a second reads as
   imprecise - the conservative side.)
3. **Legacy records** (no per-window keys): the window instants are UNKNOWN (`EndpointWindow.
   window_legacy`; the aggregate stands in only for the legacy-vs-legacy comparison). A legacy window
   never wins on recency against a window with a known instant - that pair is decided by the 8d rank
   alone; no per-window key is written for a legacy window.
Tests: `a_subsecond_instant_survives_the_record_and_beats_an_older_live_one`,
`a_second_precision_record_ties_with_a_live_instant_of_the_same_second`,
`a_legacy_record_never_wins_on_recency_against_a_known_instant` (replaces the 8h legacy test; the
health verdict sees the block). Pairwise comparisons mixing precise and imprecise instants are not
strictly transitive across three or more observations within one second; the rank keeps each pair
deterministic. The plugin's T17 fix needs the same three rules.

## 8j - ONE total order per window (supersedes the 8i pairwise precision rule)

The 8i rule (whole-second compare only when a side is imprecise) was not transitive across mixed
precisions inside one second, and a legacy window decided by rank against known ones broke the fold
the same way. Now every instant comparison in the selection and the merge is made at WHOLE-SECOND
granularity (`cmp_instants`: floor to the second; fractions are never an ordering key): a strictly
later second wins on recency; the same second is a tie that `cmp_window_rank` (8d) decides. The
fractional instants stay stored, re-stamped and round-tripped exactly (8i) - bookkeeping, not a
key. Within one kind of window (known instants, or legacy aggregates compared at the same
granularity) (floor second, rank) is a lexicographic total order. The legacy rule stays - an unknown
instant never wins on recency against a known one, the rank alone decides - and to keep the fold
order-independent `select_window` keeps the best KNOWN and the best LEGACY candidate per window
(`EndpointWindow` slots) and resolves the visible window from that pair (the legacy one only if it
outranks the known one by the rank), so the pick is a function of the candidate SET. Inside one
second the higher-usage window wins: the conservative side (usage only rises within a window; a
reset is already ranked by future/past). Tests: `whole_second_order_is_transitive_for_the_abc_precision_case`
(a imprecise :00 50 %, b :00.100 99 %, c :00.900 30 %, six orders -> 99 %),
`mixed_precision_candidates_give_one_pick_in_every_order` (six candidates - two imprecise, two with
fractions in one second, one in the next second, one legacy, partial windows - 720 orders through
the recorded selection and `merge_observation`, plus a recorded/live split); the 8i sub-second test
now passes by rank (99 % at :00.900 against live 30 % at :00.100). The plugin's T17 fix uses the
same total order.

# Handoff 01 - claude: framing panel A - measuring reviewers and workers (usage tiers, worker telemetry)

Date: 2026-10-14. Base commit: C3 `v0.2.1` (8a133f8); the PowerShell plugin `claude-codex-consult` 0.6.1 (main
dcb9d59, wave 30 unreleased). Both are the same program: a bridge that lets a coordinating agent (Claude Code, Codex
CLI and other hosts) consult reviewer models through their CLIs, with a reviewer roster, a findings store, and an
anonymised telemetry intake at `xelth.com/T/`. Read `README.md` and `docs/port/wave8-quota.md` of this repository
for the current behaviour; the roster shape is in the README's "Reviewer roster and panel".

## Question

Before any of this is implemented, we want the panel's angle on two measurement designs that will shape the
roster, the telemetry schema and the routing for a long time: (A) usage TIERS for the two standing consultants
(OpenAI gpt-6-astra through the ChatGPT subscription, Zhipu glm-5.3 through z.ai) - which reasoning effort to
send for which purpose, and how to score a tier; (B) WORKER telemetry - the coordinator's own sub-agents (Claude
Code tiers haiku / sonnet / opus / fable AND their effort levels) counted and scored at near-zero token cost so the
tier choice can be improved from data. Both change a closed telemetry vocabulary that is hard to change once
published.

## Task state

- Done: the telemetry intake (consult and rating events; engine, vendor class, a closed list of model names, purpose,
  outcome class, counts - never a task, prompt, path or name); the quota windows (wave 8: the 5-hour and weekly
  ChatGPT windows read from the Codex rollouts; a round of review costs 8-23 % of the 5-hour window at effort high;
  a forked thread with sub-agents once cost 96 % in 186 s); effort vocabularies per endpoint (caps-v1: openai
  low|medium|high|xhigh; z.ai low|high|max with medium->high and xhigh->max); purpose presets (chore low, checkpoint
  medium, acceptance high, core-contract/stuck xhigh); the ratings (`rate`, `useful yes|partly|no`) per
  consultation; a routed panel seats reviewers by track record.
- Open: no telemetry event carries the effort; no event exists for workers at all; the roster has no per-purpose
  effort policy per entry; nothing measures a tier against its cost.
- Not in scope: new reviewer engines; the browser engine; the intake's hosting.

## Evidence

- `crates/c3/src/telemetry/classes.rs` - the closed vocabulary of the events (what can be added without breaking
  the published schema).
- `crates/c3-core/src/quota.rs` - what a run costs in window share and tokens (`tokens`, `quota`, `budget` in the
  ledger entry): the cost side of a score exists per consultation already.
- `.collab/parity-0.6.1-2026-10-08/state.md`, sections "Planned (2026-10-14 10:40): usage tiers" and "Planned
  after the tag: worker telemetry" - the coordinator's current sketch (below).
- Observed today: nine review rounds of one wave with gpt-6-astra at effort high found one real defect each
  (F46-1 .. F62-1), 183-234 s and 10-15 % of the 5-hour window per round; a GLM round at `max` is cheaper in money
  and has no 5-hour window; Claude Code workers (opus / sonnet) did each fix in 15-70 minutes.

## The coordinator's sketch (to be challenged)

(A) Usage tiers. Roster entries get an effort POLICY per purpose (e.g. gpt-6-astra: chore medium, reading pass
medium, diff-review high, core-contract xhigh; glm-5.3: chore low, review high, stuck max). The consult and
rating events carry `effort` (the tier SENT after the vocabulary mapping - closed: none|low|medium|high|xhigh|max)
and `effort_requested` (the preset name). The intake's usefulness table splits per reviewer x effort. Routing
"scout and judge": a cheap tier (GLM low, or a Haiku worker) reads the diff and writes a digest handoff; the judge
(Astra high, or GLM max) gets the digest plus a call cap; the digest survives a cold cache. Open: does z.ai expose
more than three tiers on glm-5.3; is `medium` on gpt-6-astra good enough for a reading pass; how to SCORE a tier -
usefulness per 5-hour-window share, not per run.

(B) Worker telemetry. Claude Code's `SubagentStop` hook (the plugin can ship it) fires at each worker's end with
the agent type; the bridge records one closed-class event per worker: tier (haiku|sonnet|opus|fable|other), effort
level if the host exposes it, duration class, outcome class (reported | stopped-by-coordinator | error | unknown),
and a coordinator-side mark after the fact (`c3 workers rate <id> useful yes|partly|no`) - never the brief, the
files or the repository. The intake gets a "workers" table (counts, error share, usefulness per tier x effort).
Cost: one hook invocation per worker, no model tokens. Open: can the hook see the effort and the tier reliably
(agent definition vs model alias); how to attribute a wave's success to a worker when the coordinator reworked it;
what a user of another host (Codex CLI agents, Kimi) can report.

## Alternatives weighed

1. **Effort policy in the roster + effort in the events (the sketch)** - small schema change now; the score needs
   months of data.
2. **No new telemetry; a local experiment first** (the coordinator runs the same brief at two efforts for a week and
   compares findings per window share) - no schema risk; nothing learned for other users.
3. **Score reviewers by findings confirmed, not by usefulness marks** - more objective (a finding later marked
   `implemented`/`verified` is a hit); needs the findings store joined to the events (ids are private today).
4. **Workers: no hook, the coordinator's own notes in STATE.md** - zero code; not comparable across users.

Current preference: 1 for reviewers with the window-share denominator; 3 as the long-term score once the findings
join exists; for workers the hook with closed classes, but only if the effort is visible to it.

120	Goal: know which worker tier (opus / sonnet / haiku / other) did what kind of work and how it ended, across installs
121	(users on an Opus-max or a Sonnet-max plan), WITHOUT spending the coordinator's tokens. Design:
122	- The signal source is the host's hook, not the model: Claude Code runs `SubagentStop` (and `SubagentStart`) hooks
123	  as shell commands with a JSON on stdin (session, transcript paths, the agent id - to verify: `agent_transcript_path`).
124	  C3 ships `c3 hook subagent-stop`; the plugin ships the PowerShell mirror in its hooks.json. Zero model tokens.
125	- From the subagent's transcript the hook computes CLASSES AND NUMBERS only: tier (the plugin's agent names
126	  opus-worker/sonnet-worker/haiku-worker, else `other`), the actual model (closed list of published names, else
127	  `other`), outcome (`completed`, `error:rate_limit`, `error:context` (prompt too long), `error:other`, `stopped`),
128	  duration bucket, input/output token buckets, tool-use count bucket, tool-error count bucket, edits bucket
129	  (Edit/Write calls -> `read-only` vs `writes`), whether a verification command ran (cargo test / pytest / run-all
130	  patterns -> `verified`), resumes (SendMessage continuations of the same agent). Never a prompt, a path, a name.
131	- Optional judgment at ~50 tokens: `c3 worker rate <agent id> yes|partly|no --note` (mirrors `-Rate` for reviewers);
132	  the event carries the mark like the reviewer rating (`rating_rev`, judge).

136	- Cost: hook CPU only; the rating is optional. Privacy as the existing contract (closed classes, consult_ref-style

## Planned after the tag: worker telemetry (the operator's request, 2026-10-13 22:40)

Goal: know which worker tier (opus / sonnet / haiku / other) did what kind of work and how it ended, across installs
(users on an Opus-max or a Sonnet-max plan), WITHOUT spending the coordinator's tokens. Design:
- The signal source is the host's hook, not the model: Claude Code runs `SubagentStop` (and `SubagentStart`) hooks
  as shell commands with a JSON on stdin (session, transcript paths, the agent id - to verify: `agent_transcript_path`).
  C3 ships `c3 hook subagent-stop`; the plugin ships the PowerShell mirror in its hooks.json. Zero model tokens.
- From the subagent's transcript the hook computes CLASSES AND NUMBERS only: tier (the plugin's agent names
  opus-worker/sonnet-worker/haiku-worker, else `other`), the actual model (closed list of published names, else
  `other`), outcome (`completed`, `error:rate_limit`, `error:context` (prompt too long), `error:other`, `stopped`),
  duration bucket, input/output token buckets, tool-use count bucket, tool-error count bucket, edits bucket
  (Edit/Write calls -> `read-only` vs `writes`), whether a verification command ran (cargo test / pytest / run-all
  patterns -> `verified`), resumes (SendMessage continuations of the same agent). Never a prompt, a path, a name.
- Optional judgment at ~50 tokens: `c3 worker rate <agent id> yes|partly|no --note` (mirrors `-Rate` for reviewers);
  the event carries the mark like the reviewer rating (`rating_rev`, judge).
- One event per subagent end to the intake (event class `worker`); the intake (xelth.com crates/telemetry) gets the
  schema and a public table "workers": per tier x outcome counts, error share, median duration/tokens, the rating
  share - so a user can see whether e.g. sonnet-worker finishes verification waves as often as opus-worker.
- Cost: hook CPU only; the rating is optional. Privacy as the existing contract (closed classes, consult_ref-style
  pseudonymous keys). Order: after v0.2.0 - C3 wave "worker telemetry", the plugin mirror, the intake + page.

The brief treats (A) and (B) as two measurement designs. They are one decision: both need the same two axes - a normalized effort token and an actor/tier class - added to a closed vocabulary. Decide that once, not twice.

Options the brief does not list: (O5) record nothing new now - the local ledger already holds `effort`, `effort_requested`, `effort_mapping`, `effort_caps` (`crates/c3-core/src/ledger.rs:195`), and `crates/c3/src/telemetry/backfill.rs` shows backfill is a paved road; write the events once you know the fields. (O6) Make effort a randomized router arm (epsilon-exploration), so the score falls out of decisions you must make anyway. (O7) A paired design: the same brief at two tiers on the same diff - the only cheap route to identified causal data.

To choose I would need: how many usable cells you will really have in three months; whether the intake rejects unknown keys and carries a schema version; whether Astra's window share is attributable per run at all.

## Q1 - tiers and the denominator
gpt-6-astra: nothing below `high` for a run that yields a verdict; `medium` only for a mechanical reading pass over a diff you already trust; `xhigh` for core-contract/stuck only. The only evidence is nine hits at `high`; `medium` for a reading pass is an untested bet - pair it (O7) rather than assume it. glm-5.3: the three tiers are the vendor's cap (`crates/c3-core/src/effort.rs:101`), so `low`=chore, `high`=review, `max`=stuck. The denominator: none is universal. Astra's window is shared with the operator's other traffic (8 to 72 % with no bridge runs, `state.md:208`), so use the marginal change around the run, not the nominal share; GLM has no window at all, so compare on money or wall time only. Confirmed findings (option 3) is the right long-term numerator, but usefulness marks are chosen by the coordinator who chose the tier - they measure the chooser.

## Q2 - capture point, privacy, attribution
`SubagentStop` is necessary and not sufficient: it does not fire for a worker the coordinator kills or one that dies with the process, so `stopped`/`error` - the shares the table exists to show - are under-counted. Pair it with `SubagentStart` and reconcile at wave end (Start without Stop implies stopped/unknown). An Agent call's effort override is probably absent from the transcript: take effort from the coordinator or send `unknown`, never guess. Keep out: brief or prompt text, paths (`agent_transcript_path` stays local), the agent label as typed, session/agent ids (pseudonymise like `consult_ref`), the `--note` text, tool arguments, repo and cwd. Attribution: the hook sees execution, not survival. Add a coordinator-side post-hoc class - `as-delivered | reworked | superseded | unused` - and attribute primarily at the wave (did the wave pass, in how many attempts).

## Q3 - fields to add now
- `vocab_version`: the event must name the mapping that produced the tier; `CAPS_VERSION` exists locally (`crates/c3-core/src/effort.rs:5`) and has no place on the wire.
- `effort` (sent) + `effort_requested` + `effort_mapping`: z.ai maps `medium` and `high` to the single sent value `high` (`crates/c3/src/consult/orchestrate.rs:1193`), so the sent token alone cannot tell the two apart - exactly the comparison you want.
- `actor` (`reviewer|worker|coordinator`), `tier` (`haiku|sonnet|opus|fable|other`), `host` class - one event family, not two tables.
- `billing` class plus an optional window share: an absent denominator must be legal, not zero.
- `wave_id` and `attempt_index` (pseudonymous) to join rework.
Anti-breakage is permissive ingest plus a version, not more fields: the payload is a fixed struct with an exact-bytes test (`crates/c3/src/telemetry/classes.rs:267`), so accept-and-ignore unknown keys before the first new field ships.

## Q4 - scout and judge
It fails where the scout's false negative is invisible: the judge can only audit what the digest contains, and shrinking the digest drops the anchors that would let the judge contradict it. A cold-cache digest that does not name its commit lets the judge reason on a moved tree. Cap items (at most N) and per-item quote length, not bytes; demand one anchor per claim and a what-I-did-not-read coverage count; let the judge open N anchors itself; make `digest insufficient, escalate to full read` a counted outcome; and run the occasional unassisted control to measure the scout's miss rate.

.collab/consilium-2026-10-14/handoffs\03-codex-panel-a-measure-kimi.reply.json:1:{"schema_version":"1","verdict":"ADVISE","verdict_reason":"The sketch's two parts differ in risk: extending the closed vocabulary is safe (every list already degrades to `other`), but the scoring denominators and the worker-effort capture assumption are not yet sound enough to publish.","reply_markdown":"## Framing challenge first

The brief bundles one safe decision with two unsafe ones. Extending the closed vocabulary is nearly free: `classes.rs` already maps anything unknown to `other`/`unknown`, so new values never break old intakes. The risky parts are (a) committing to a *published score* before the denominators are comparable, and (b) assuming the hook can see effort.

Options the brief does not list:

- **(5) Tier-split panels as the experiment.** Alternative 2 (local A/B) is dismissed as "nothing learned for other users" — but the routed panel already exists. Send the same brief at two efforts to two seats of one panel; the existing consult events capture it for everyone once `effort` ships. This is alternative 1 and 2 combined, at panel cost.
- **(6) Publish counts, keep scores local.** `c3 scoreboard` is already local. Ship only `effort` on events and let each install compute its own usefulness-per-cost; the intake publishes distributions, not rankings. Defers the irreversible "published metric" decision until the findings join (alternative 3) exists.
- **(7) Record effort now, commit to no score at all.** Schema first, semantics later.

What I would need to choose: does z.ai expose more than three glm-5.3 tiers; does `SubagentStop` stdin (or the transcript metadata) carry the Agent call's effort override; how is the intake schema versioned today.

## Q1 — tiers and denominator

Tiers: gpt-6-astra (window-bound): chore low, checkpoint/reading medium, diff-review/acceptance high, core-contract/stuck xhigh. glm-5.3 (money-bound, no 5-hour window): chore low, everything else high, stuck max — the asymmetry is real and the policy should encode it. Denominator: findings-confirmed per unit of the *binding constraint* — window-share for OpenAI, money for GLM, wall time only as a guard. Finding F1: window share is not a cross-vendor denominator (quota.rs reads Codex rollouts only), so "usefulness per window share" cannot be the single published score. Design not listed: score the **marginal finding** — findings no other panel seat produced — per cost unit; it survives routed panels where seats differ.

## Q2 — worker capture

`SubagentStop` is the right capture point for Claude Code; other hosts report via the coordinator's own `rate` path with tier `other`. Must stay out: transcript/cwd/repo paths, session id (hash it), the agent label as typed. Effort: do not trust the transcript — the coordinator knows effort at spawn; have it write a local worker-id→{tier,effort} registry the hook reads (zero tokens, no parsing). Attribution under rework: add outcome `reworked`, marked at rating time; credit completion to the last worker, charge the rework against the original tier's score. Without this the original tier's completion share is inflated (F5).

## Q3 — add to the vocabulary now

`effort` (sent, closed none|low|medium|high|xhigh|max), `effort_requested` (preset name or `other`), `effort_native` (pre-mapping label — otherwise medium→high is indistinguishable from native high later, F2), `cost_basis` (window|money|none) so denominators stay interpretable, and `schema_v` per event. Worker event: tier, effort, outcome class, duration/token buckets, verified flag, resume count, reworked flag.

## Q4 — scout and judge

Failure modes: the scout summarizes the anomaly away; the judge anchors on the scout's conclusion; a cold-cache digest silently drops context. Rules: the scout emits a **fixed schema**, never a verdict — file list, hunk ids, suspicion 0–3 per hunk — capped at ~200 lines; the judge always gets the raw file list and may fetch the raw diff of any hunk (a tool call, not a bigger digest). The brief treats (A) and (B) as two measurement designs. They are one decision: both need the same two axes - a normalized effort token and an actor/tier class - added to a closed vocabulary. Decide that once, not twice.

Options the brief does not list: (O5) record nothing new now - the local ledger already holds `effort`, `effort_requested`, `effort_mapping`, `effort_caps` (`crates/c3-core/src/ledger.rs:195`), and `crates/c3/src/telemetry/backfill.rs` shows backfill is a paved road; write the events once you know the fields. (O6) Make effort a randomized router arm (epsilon-exploration), so the score falls out of decisions you must make anyway. (O7) A paired design: the same brief at two tiers on the same diff - the only cheap route to identified causal data.

To choose I would need: how many usable cells you will really have in three months; whether the intake rejects unknown keys and carries a schema version; whether Astra's window share is attributable per run at all.

## Q1 - tiers and the denominator
gpt-6-astra: nothing below `high` for a run that yields a verdict; `medium` only for a mechanical reading pass over a diff you already trust; `xhigh` for core-contract/stuck only. The only evidence is nine hits at `high`; `medium` for a reading pass is an untested bet - pair it (O7) rather than assume it. glm-5.3: the three tiers are the vendor's cap (`crates/c3-core/src/effort.rs:101`), so `low`=chore, `high`=review, `max`=stuck. The denominator: none is universal. Astra's window is shared with the operator's other traffic (8 to 72 % with no bridge runs, `state.md:208`), so use the marginal change around the run, not the nominal share; GLM has no window at all, so compare on money or wall time only. Confirmed findings (option 3) is the right long-term numerator, but usefulness marks are chosen by the coordinator who chose the tier - they measure the chooser.

## Q2 - capture point, privacy, attribution
`SubagentStop` is necessary and not sufficient: it does not fire for a worker the coordinator kills or one that dies with the process, so `stopped`/`error` - the shares the table exists to show - are under-counted. Pair it with `SubagentStart` and reconcile at wave end (Start without Stop implies stopped/unknown). An Agent call's effort override is probably absent from the transcript: take effort from the coordinator or send `unknown`, never guess. Keep out: brief or prompt text, paths (`agent_transcript_path` stays local), the agent label as typed, session/agent ids (pseudonymise like `consult_ref`), the `--note` text, tool arguments, repo and cwd. Attribution: the hook sees execution, not survival. Add a coordinator-side post-hoc class - `as-delivered | reworked | superseded | unused` - and attribute primarily at the wave (did the wave pass, in how many attempts).

## Q3 - fields to add now
- `vocab_version`: the event must name the mapping that produced the tier; `CAPS_VERSION` exists locally (`crates/c3-core/src/effort.rs:5`) and has no place on the wire.
- `effort` (sent) + `effort_requested` + `effort_mapping`: z.ai maps `medium` and `high` to the single sent value `high` (`crates/c3/src/consult/orchestrate.rs:1193`), so the sent token alone cannot tell the two apart - exactly the comparison you want.
- `actor` (`reviewer|worker|coordinator`), `tier` (`haiku|sonnet|opus|fable|other`), `host` class - one event family, not two tables.
- `billing` class plus an optional window share: an absent denominator must be legal, not zero.
- `wave_id` and `attempt_index` (pseudonymous) to join rework.
Anti-breakage is permissive ingest plus a version, not more fields: the payload is a fixed struct with an exact-bytes test (`crates/c3/src/telemetry/classes.rs:267`), so accept-and-ignore unknown keys before the first new field ships.

## Q4 - scout and judge
It fails where the scout's false negative is invisible: the judge can only audit what the digest contains, and shrinking the digest drops the anchors that would let the judge contradict it. A cold-cache digest that does not name its commit lets the judge reason on a moved tree. Cap items (at most N) and per-item quote length, not bytes; demand one anchor per claim and a what-I-did-not-read coverage count; let the judge open N anchors itself; make `digest insufficient, escalate to full read` a counted outcome; and run the occasional unassisted control to measure the scout's miss rate.

.collab/consilium-2026-10-14/handoffs\03-codex-panel-a-measure-kimi.original.md:3:{"schema_version":"1","verdict":"ADVISE","verdict_reason":"The sketch's two parts differ in risk: extending the closed vocabulary is safe (every list already degrades to `other`), but the scoring denominators and the worker-effort capture assumption are not yet sound enough to publish.","reply_markdown":"## Framing challenge first

The brief bundles one safe decision with two unsafe ones. Extending the closed vocabulary is nearly free: `classes.rs` already maps anything unknown to `other`/`unknown`, so new values never break old intakes. The risky parts are (a) committing to a *published score* before the denominators are comparable, and (b) assuming the hook can see effort.

Options the brief does not list:

- **(5) Tier-split panels as the experiment.** Alternative 2 (local A/B) is dismissed as "nothing learned for other users" — but the routed panel already exists. Send the same brief at two efforts to two seats of one panel; the existing consult events capture it for everyone once `effort` ships. This is alternative 1 and 2 combined, at panel cost.
- **(6) Publish counts, keep scores local.** `c3 scoreboard` is already local. Ship only `effort` on events and let each install compute its own usefulness-per-cost; the intake publishes distributions, not rankings. Defers the irreversible "published metric" decision until the findings join (alternative 3) exists.
- **(7) Record effort now, commit to no score at all.** Schema first, semantics later.

What I would need to choose: does z.ai expose more than three glm-5.3 tiers; does `SubagentStop` stdin (or the transcript metadata) carry the Agent call's effort override; how is the intake schema versioned today.

## Q1 — tiers and denominator

Tiers: gpt-6-astra (window-bound): chore low, checkpoint/reading medium, diff-review/acceptance high, core-contract/stuck xhigh. glm-5.3 (money-bound, no 5-hour window): chore low, everything else high, stuck max — the asymmetry is real and the policy should encode it. Denominator: findings-confirmed per unit of the *binding constraint* — window-share for OpenAI, money for GLM, wall time only as a guard. Finding F1: window share is not a cross-vendor denominator (quota.rs reads Codex rollouts only), so "usefulness per window share" cannot be the single published score. Design not listed: score the **marginal finding** — findings no other panel seat produced — per cost unit; it survives routed panels where seats differ.

## Q2 — worker capture

`SubagentStop` is the right capture point for Claude Code; other hosts report via the coordinator's own `rate` path with tier `other`. Must stay out: transcript/cwd/repo paths, session id (hash it), the agent label as typed. Effort: do not trust the transcript — the coordinator knows effort at spawn; have it write a local worker-id→{tier,effort} registry the hook reads (zero tokens, no parsing). Attribution under rework: add outcome `reworked`, marked at rating time; credit completion to the last worker, charge the rework against the original tier's score. # Handoff 01 - claude: framing panel A - measuring reviewers and workers (usage tiers, worker telemetry)

Date: 2026-10-14. Base commit: C3 `v0.2.1` (8a133f8); the PowerShell plugin `claude-codex-consult` 0.6.1 (main
dcb9d59, wave 30 unreleased). Both are the same program: a bridge that lets a coordinating agent (Claude Code, Codex
CLI and other hosts) consult reviewer models through their CLIs, with a reviewer roster, a findings store, and an
anonymised telemetry intake at `xelth.com/T/`. Read `README.md` and `docs/port/wave8-quota.md` of this repository
for the current behaviour; the roster shape is in the README's "Reviewer roster and panel".

## Question

Before any of this is implemented, we want the panel's angle on two measurement designs that will shape the
roster, the telemetry schema and the routing for a long time: (A) usage TIERS for the two standing consultants
(OpenAI gpt-6-astra through the ChatGPT subscription, Zhipu glm-5.3 through z.ai) - which reasoning effort to
send for which purpose, and how to score a tier; (B) WORKER telemetry - the coordinator's own sub-agents (Claude
Code tiers haiku / sonnet / opus / fable AND their effort levels) counted and scored at near-zero token cost so the
tier choice can be improved from data. Both change a closed telemetry vocabulary that is hard to change once
published.

## Task state

- Done: the telemetry intake (consult and rating events; engine, vendor class, a closed list of model names, purpose,
  outcome class, counts - never a task, prompt, path or name); the quota windows (wave 8: the 5-hour and weekly
  ChatGPT windows read from the Codex rollouts; a round of review costs 8-23 % of the 5-hour window at effort high;
  a forked thread with sub-agents once cost 96 % in 186 s); effort vocabularies per endpoint (caps-v1: openai
  low|medium|high|xhigh; z.ai low|high|max with medium->high and xhigh->max); purpose presets (chore low, checkpoint
  medium, acceptance high, core-contract/stuck xhigh); the ratings (`rate`, `useful yes|partly|no`) per
  consultation; a routed panel seats reviewers by track record.
- Open: no telemetry event carries the effort; no event exists for workers at all; the roster has no per-purpose
  effort policy per entry; nothing measures a tier against its cost.
- Not in scope: new reviewer engines; the browser engine; the intake's hosting.

## Evidence

- `crates/c3/src/telemetry/classes.rs` - the closed vocabulary of the events (what can be added without breaking
  the published schema).
- `crates/c3-core/src/quota.rs` - what a run costs in window share and tokens (`tokens`, `quota`, `budget` in the
  ledger entry): the cost side of a score exists per consultation already.
- `.collab/parity-0.6.1-2026-10-08/state.md`, sections "Planned (2026-10-14 10:40): usage tiers" and "Planned
  after the tag: worker telemetry" - the coordinator's current sketch (below).
- Observed today: nine review rounds of one wave with gpt-6-astra at effort high found one real defect each
  (F46-1 .. F62-1), 183-234 s and 10-15 % of the 5-hour window per round; a GLM round at `max` is cheaper in money
  and has no 5-hour window; Claude Code workers (opus / sonnet) did each fix in 15-70 minutes.

## The coordinator's sketch (to be challenged)

(A) Usage tiers. Roster entries get an effort POLICY per purpose (e.g. gpt-6-astra: chore medium, reading pass
medium, diff-review high, core-contract xhigh; glm-5.3: chore low, review high, stuck max). The consult and
rating events carry `effort` (the tier SENT after the vocabulary mapping - closed: none|low|medium|high|xhigh|max)
and `effort_requested` (the preset name). The intake's usefulness table splits per reviewer x effort. Routing
"scout and judge": a cheap tier (GLM low, or a Haiku worker) reads the diff and writes a digest handoff; the judge
(Astra high, or GLM max) gets the digest plus a call cap; the digest survives a cold cache. Open: does z.ai expose
more than three tiers on glm-5.3; is `medium` on gpt-6-astra good enough for a reading pass; how to SCORE a tier -
usefulness per 5-hour-window share, not per run.

(B) Worker telemetry. Claude Code's `SubagentStop` hook (the plugin can ship it) fires at each worker's end with
the agent type; the bridge records one closed-class event per worker: tier (haiku|sonnet|opus|fable|other), effort
level if the host exposes it, duration class, outcome class (reported | stopped-by-coordinator | error | unknown),
and a coordinator-side mark after the fact (`c3 workers rate <id> useful yes|partly|no`) - never the brief, the
files or the repository. The intake gets a "workers" table (counts, error share, usefulness per tier x effort).
Cost: one hook invocation per worker, no model tokens. Open: can the hook see the effort and the tier reliably
(agent definition vs model alias); how to attribute a wave's success to a worker when the coordinator reworked it;
what a user of another host (Codex CLI agents, Kimi) can report.

## Alternatives weighed

1. **Effort policy in the roster + effort in the events (the sketch)** - small schema change now; the score needs
   months of data.
2. **No new telemetry; a local experiment first** (the coordinator runs the same brief at two efforts for a week and
   compares findings per window share) - no schema risk; nothing learned for other users.
3. **Score reviewers by findings confirmed, not by usefulness marks** - more objective (a finding later marked
   `implemented`/`verified` is a hit); needs the findings store joined to the events (ids are private today).
4. **Workers: no hook, the coordinator's own notes in STATE.md** - zero code; not comparable across users.

Current preference: 1 for reviewers with the window-share denominator; 3 as the long-term score once the findings
join exists; for workers the hook with closed classes, but only if the effort is visible to it.

## Questions

- **Q1.** For (A): which effort tiers would you send per purpose for gpt-6-astra and glm-5.3, and what is the right
  denominator to score a tier (window share, money, wall time, findings confirmed)? Name a design we did not list.
- **Q2.** For (B): is the SubagentStop hook the right capture point; what MUST stay out of the event for privacy;
  and how would you attribute a worker's result when the coordinator reworks it?
- **Q3.** The schema: which fields would you add to the closed vocabulary now so we never have to break it later?
- **Q4.** The "scout and judge" routing: where does it fail (a digest that hides the defect), and what cap on the
  scout's output keeps the judge honest?

## Quota windows and the reading budget (plugin wave 30; C3 wave 8)

A subscription's quota is spent in windows - on a ChatGPT plan a 5-hour window and a weekly one -
and ONE review can spend a whole 5-hour window: a fork replays its parent's context on every tool
call, and a reviewer's own sub-agents replay theirs. C3 reads what Codex itself writes into each
thread's rollout (`<codex home>/sessions/<yyyy>/<mm>/<dd>/rollout-<ts>-<thread>.jsonl`, the last
`token_count` that names a window) and acts on it, as the plugin does (`docs/port/wave8-quota.md`):

- **Ledger** (codex runs, after `commit_wait_ms`): `quota {primary, secondary, observed_at}`,
  `tokens {input, cached, output, thread_input, calls, max_input, context_window, subagents {count,
  input, calls}}` (the run's share of the thread's running total - a fork inherits its parent's),
  `subagents_allowed`, `budget`; the summary's `quota      :` line and the handoff's
  `Quota (rollout):` line.
- **Verdict**: the newest observed window of an endpoint (its ledgers, the machine-wide health
  records - which now carry `quota` - and, for the built-in `openai` endpoint while the
  machine-wide health is on, the codex home's newest rollout): at 98 % or more with its reset ahead
  the endpoint is `unavailable (5-hour window 99 % used, resets <iso>)` like a usage limit with a
  known reset (roster walk, `--require`, panel, `--short`, a real run refused); at 80 % or more the
  verdict says `available (low quota: 5-hour window 84 % until 18:32)`. `c3 providers` has a QUOTA
  column (`5h 96% until 18:32; wk 15% until Oct 20`) and `--json` rows a `quota` object.
- **`--budget <percent>`** (env `CODEX_CONSULT_QUOTA_BUDGET`, default 90, 0 = off): the stall watch
  reads the run's rollout every 15 s and stops the main turn at the budget - the partial kept, no
  continuation, `failed: stopped at the quota budget: 5-hour window 91 % used, resets 18:32; the
  partial is kept` (provider_failure class `operator`, telemetry class `quota`).
- **Replay guard**: a `--mode fork|resume` whose parent rollout is over `CODEX_CONSULT_FORK_MAX_KB`
  (default 512) is refused before anything starts; from 128 KB on it is warned about.
- **Sub-agents off**: every codex turn passes `-c features.multi_agent=false` right after `-m`
  unless `--codex-config` (or the roster's `codex_config`) names `features.multi_agent`.
- **Reading discipline**: the purpose paragraphs of acceptance, diff-review, checkpoint and
  core-contract end with the plugin's block (`git diff <range> --stat` first, one path at a time
  with a line cap, the documents first, the verdict even on an incomplete read).

## Telemetry (on by default, off with one line)

Installing C3 means accepting these terms. C3 reports **one anonymous event per
consultation** (and one per usefulness rating) to the maintainer's intake,
<https://xelth.com/T/>, so the bridge can be improved when someone the maintainer never hears
from uses it. Everything collected is shown in the open, as counts, on <https://xelth.com/C3/>.

* **Sent - classes only:** `app_id` (`c3`), the C3 version, an instance id
  (`sha256(salt file + machine name)` â€” stable per installation, meaningless elsewhere), a
  severity, and `details`: the engine, the reviewer's VENDOR CLASS and model (below), the purpose
  (one of the eight purposes, `none` or `other`), the outcome class (`usable`,
  `usable-after-continuation`, `failed:<class>` with a closed class), wall seconds, token counts,
  findings counts, structured or not, a format retry or not, panel size, the federation peer
  COUNT, OS, runtime, and `consult_ref` (below). `tags` repeat `[provider, model]`.
* **The rating event** (`c3 findings --rate`, `c3 telemetry --backfill-ratings`): `details` exactly
  `engine, provider, model, purpose, mark, age_days, bridge_version, os, ps_version, judge,
  rating_rev, consult_ref` (the plugin's 0.6.1 shape; `ps_version` is `unknown` - C3 runs no
  PowerShell), `title` the mark, `client_time` the MARK's own time on every path. `judge` is
  `{provider, model, source}` - who gave the mark, resolved at rating time and saved in the mark:
  `rating_actor` (`CODEX_CONSULT_COORDINATOR` of the rating process), `consult_coordinator` (the
  coordinator the consultation recorded) or `unknown` - classes only, never a label or a host.
  `rating_rev` is the mark's revision (1 + the consultation's highest); the intake keeps per
  `(instance_id, consult_ref)` the rating with the highest `rating_rev`.
* **`consult_ref`:** a random id minted for each consultation (a lower-case guid, derived from
  nothing - not the `consult_id` the reviewer sees), kept in the ledger right after `consult_id`
  and sent in the consultation event and every rating event of it, so the intake can link them.
  A pseudonymous correlation key: whoever holds both the telemetry and a shared `sessions.json`
  can join them on it.
* **The classes** (the plugin's closed vendor table; `c3/src/telemetry/classes.rs`): the vendor
  class is derived from the HOST of the endpoint the reviewer talked to (`openai` - also Codex's
  built-in provider -, `zai`, `xiaomi`, `byteplus`, `moonshot`, `alibaba`, `minimax`), else from
  the engine (`agy` google, `muse` meta, `claude` anthropic), else `other`; the model is sent only
  when it EQUALS an entry of that class's closed list (after lower-casing, `[1m]` stripped),
  else `other` (`unknown` without a model). A roster label, a model or a purpose as typed - say
  `customer-acme` - never leaves the machine. **C3 extension (the `http` engine):** the host
  `openrouter.ai` is the class `openrouter`; its model is sent in OpenRouter's `<vendor>/<model>`
  form only when the vendor slug is one of `openai`, `anthropic`, `google`, `z-ai`, `moonshotai`,
  `minimax`, `xiaomi`, `qwen` (alibaba's list), `meta-llama` (meta's list) AND the model part
  equals an entry of that class's list (`openai/gpt-5.1`), else `other`; an http endpoint of a
  listed vendor's host takes that vendor's class, any other host `other`.
* **Never:** task names, prompts, briefs, paths, thread ids, `consult_id`, finding texts, notes,
  topics, labels as typed, the coordinator's host, user names, keys. The server drops
  secret-named keys on arrival and reports how many; C3 treats a non-zero count as its own bug.
* **Off:** `CODEX_CONSULT_TELEMETRY=off` (any value other than unset/`on`/`1`/`true`/`yes`
  counts as off), or `--telemetry off` per run - a run's own `--telemetry on|off` wins over the
  variable, and a panel passes it to its members. The first run after an install prints this
  notice once; the dry run says whether it is on.
* **Never blocks a run; never lost silently:** events queue in C3's own outbox
  (`<codex home>/c3/telemetry/spool.ndjson`, one `{v, kind, queued_unix, body}` line each - not
  the plugin's `telemetry-spool/`: C3 is its own app with its own salt and instance id), are sent
  by a detached sender a run starts right after its commit (a consultation, a panel - once -, a
  rating, a backfill; the run never waits for it, and it gets an allow-listed environment only: no
  key, no host marker) in batches of at most 100 (one flush ends after 60 s, one request after 8 s),
  retried by the next sender and dropped 7 days after they were queued. The sender follows the
  intake's answers as the plugin does: a 429 whose `Retry-After` is at most 60 s is waited for
  once (else the batch stays queued), a 400 naming `events[i]` drops that event and resends the
  rest (at most three per flush), a 413 halves the batch and drops an event too large alone -
  each refused event is one line of the last flush's `rejected` - and a 403, another refusal or no
  answer stops the flush with the outbox kept. Appends and the sender are synchronised by a lock,
  and the sender removes only the lines it delivered or dropped - an event queued while it sends
  stays queued. The sender lock's owner record (`flush.owner.json`) lets `--status` and a refused
  sender say "sender busy since <t>", and after 30 minutes "sender stuck since <t> (pid <n>)". An event that cannot be
  spooled is said and counted (`c3 telemetry --status`); a rating's event is retried and else
  left for `c3 telemetry --backfill-ratings`.
* **Complaints:** `c3 --complain "<text>"` prints the exact payload (your text plus the last
  ledger entry's summary - classes only), asks before sending, and prints a public reference
  like `T-7KQ4-M2XZ` to quote on the forum section <https://xelth.com/F/p/c3> or in a mail.
* **Delete my data:** `c3 forget-me` (or `c3 telemetry --forget --public-ref <ref> [--local]`,
  or `DELETE https://xelth.com/T/v2/instances/<instance_id>?public_ref=<ref>`) asks the intake to
  remove every event and complaint this installation ever sent - proved by a complaint's public
  reference - and removes the local salt, outbox and references only AFTER the intake confirmed
  it. A DELETE the intake does not confirm deletes nothing locally: the instance id and the
  reference stay, the pending deletion is recorded (`forget-pending.json`) and nothing is
  spooled or sent until `c3 forget-me` retries it with the same identity and the intake
  confirms. Without any public reference the intake cannot verify ownership:
  `c3 forget-me --local` (or `c3 telemetry --forget --local`) removes the local data only, and
  says that the intake keeps what was sent.
* **`c3 telemetry`:** `--status` (the switch and its source, the intake, the outbox, the events
  not spooled since the last flush, the sender lock's owner, a pending deletion, the last flush,
  the instance id),
  `--flush`, `--forget`, `--backfill-ratings [--dry-run]`. The intake is
  `CODEX_CONSULT_TELEMETRY_URL` when set (https only; plain http only to a loopback host in test
  mode), else `https://xelth.com/T`.

Client rules and a 30-line Rust reference client:
[xelth.com/docs/t-hub](https://github.com/xelth-com/xelth.com/tree/main/docs/t-hub).

## Build

```sh
cargo build --release          # target/release/c3
./target/release/c3 --version
./target/release/c3 providers --short   # the reviewer availability line
cargo test && cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo build --no-default-features   # fast dev loop: drops SurrealDB (`c3 index` reports `none`)
```

The `index-surreal` feature (on by default) pulls in SurrealDB, which adds ~26 min to a
cold release build; `--no-default-features` compiles it out for a fast development loop and
CI builds both variants.

### Platforms

Windows 11 is where every harness ran and where the PowerShell plugin's evals are the oracle;
since the Linux port (`docs/port/linux-port.md`) the same tree builds, lints and tests on
Ubuntu x86_64 too, and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs fmt, clippy and the test suites on
`ubuntu-latest` and `windows-latest` (the SurrealDB build only on Ubuntu). What differs on
Linux: process liveness and the tree kill come from `/proc` and `kill` instead of the Win32
APIs and `taskkill /T`, the file locks are `flock` advisory locks instead of share modes, and
a detached run is a child in its own process group instead of a `cmd.exe` launch; the files
written are the same bytes. The tests that need Windows (cmd.exe launchers, Windows launcher
paths) are gated `#[cfg(windows)]` with a reason each. macOS is untested. For a sandbox whose
egress proxy carries the credential and re-terminates TLS, the `http` engine honours
`HTTPS_PROXY`, `C3_HTTP_AUTH_PROXY=<host,...>` (no `Authorization` header, no key read) and
`C3_HTTP_CA_BUNDLE=<pem>` (extra trust anchors) â€” see `docs/port/linux-port.md`.

A cargo workspace of three crates: `crates/c3-core` (contracts and file formats),
`crates/c3` (runtime modules), `crates/c3-cli` (the binary). Each ported piece brings its
own dependencies when it needs them; SurrealDB arrives with milestone 8 behind a feature.
The plugin's harnesses can drive the binary through `tests/shim/` (see
`docs/port/harness-shim.md`); `docs/port/m1-acceptance.md` lists the assertions milestone 1
answers to.

### Known limits (0.2.0)

- **Shared health journal with plugin 0.6.1:** with plugin 0.6.1 on the same machine the
  once-only replay of a kept journal record holds only for C3's own updates; the plugin's updater
  can re-apply a record the cap evicted until plugin 0.6.2 (its T14) - `docs/port/wave2b-compat.md`,
  "Limits".
- **Claude endpoint preflight:** the `claude --version` probe proves the launcher runs, not that it
  takes a `-p` turn; a launcher that answers `--version` but rejects the turn fails its first turn,
  and one whose `--version` needs the token is reported unavailable - `docs/port/wave4-claude.md`.
- **Claude transcript guard:** the derived location reads the child's `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, else
  `USERPROFILE` (Windows) or `HOME` (elsewhere) - Claude Code's `os.homedir()` sources - and
  refuses when neither is set; a wrapper launcher that sets `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` inside itself is
  not seen before the spawn (the strict tree check fails such a run after its turn).
- **No kill without a record:** a reviewer tree is killed only when the record naming it is on
  disk - the recovery record, its fallback or `<codex home>/c3/pending-kill/<task>-<run id>.json`;
  all three failing, the tree is left alive and the task refused while it runs. A helper left by an
  EXTERNAL death of its recorded ancestors (not by C3), below an unrecorded intermediate and with a
  command line unrelated to codex, is not detectable by either bridge -
  `docs/port/wave7-acceptance-fixes.md`, "7b".

## Install into Claude Code

`plugin/` is a Claude Code plugin directory: a `SessionStart` hook and three skills
(`consult`, `coordinate`, `setup-providers`) with brief and role templates and an `evals/`
suite â€” a thin layer over the `c3` binary built above, carrying no reviewer logic of its own.
Install the binary first (`cargo install --path crates/c3-cli`, or a release download, on
`PATH` or pointed at with `C3_EXE=<path>`), then add the plugin directory in Claude Code
(`/plugin marketplace add`, then `/plugin install`, against this repository or a local
checkout). The plugin does **not** ship the `c3 mcp` server enabled â€” a skills-driven Claude
Code session already has the surface, and an always-on server would be a second, unguided way
in; add it opt-in with a repo-root `.mcp.json` (see `docs/port/mcp.md`). See
[plugin/README.md](plugin/README.md) for the exact commands, prerequisites and how it relates
to the PowerShell [`codex-consult`](https://github.com/xelth-com/claude-codex-consult) plugin
(both can be installed side by side; their `.collab` files are byte-compatible). The
switch-over procedure from the PowerShell plugin to C3 is
[docs/port/phase2-switch.md](docs/port/phase2-switch.md).

Another Claude Code session on the same machine, from a local checkout: `claude plugin marketplace
add <path to the C3 checkout>`, then `claude plugin install c3@c3` (the marketplace is named `c3`;
user scope; other sessions pick it up at their next restart), and the binary
`cargo install --path crates/c3-cli --force` (the default build includes the local code index;
`--no-default-features` drops the `index-surreal` feature, i.e. the embedded SurrealDB index - use it
only if that feature is the problem). Once a newer plugin version is published (the version is
bumped at each release), `claude plugin update c3@c3`.
